value: A 300-pound R-134a chiller (a medium-pressure refrigerant) is to be opened for major repair with a recovery machine made in 2012. To what level must it be evacuated?
reason: Without 'major repair' (or disposal), a non-major opening not followed by evacuation to the atmosphere needs only 0 psig under §82.156(a)(1), so two answers are defensible.

value: Medium-pressure, 200 pounds or more, and equipment made on or after 15 November 1993 give the table's deepest inches figure; major repair rules out the 0 psig exception.
reason: Explanation matched to the patched front; 'after 1993' corrected to the table's 'on or after 15 November 1993'.

value: A 150-pound R-12 system (a medium-pressure refrigerant) is to be opened for major repair with a recovery machine made in 1990. To what level must it be evacuated?
reason: Without 'major repair' (or disposal), the §82.156(a)(1) non-major exception (0 psig) is an equally defensible answer.

value: Refrigerant is added on 1 March to an R-22 office chiller with a 600-pound full charge, which is found to be leaking above 10 percent; no shutdown is needed. By when must the leaks be repaired?
reason: No refrigerant or charge given; since 10 April 2020 §82.157 applies only to 50 lb or more of class I or II refrigerant, so a substitute-only chiller would owe no repair.

value: A 600-pound R-22 comfort cooling chiller leaks above 10 percent. The owner decides not to repair it but to take it out of use and replace it. What must happen within 30 days?
reason: No refrigerant given; §82.157(a) excludes appliances containing solely substitute refrigerants, so 'nothing' would also be defensible.

value: An R-22 appliance with a 400-pound full charge leaked 520 pounds during 2025. Is it a chronically leaking appliance, and what follows?
reason: No refrigerant given; the §82.157(j) report applies only within §82.157(a) scope (class I or II refrigerant).

value: The outline's item covers recharging after a repair as well as a first charge, so the leak test comes before any refrigerant goes back in.
reason: Called the test-topic item 'the rule'; the source is the outline, not the regulation.

value: B: the test topics give no same-refrigerant exception. C: the 80 percent point concerns filling cylinders in general; it does not make refilling a disposable cylinder allowed.

value: Noncondensable gas: a contaminant, measured by volume, in the rule's table of levels recycling equipment must clean refrigerant to.
reason: 'Table of contaminant limits' hides what the §82.158(k) table is: the levels that equipment sold as recycling equipment must reach.

value: The table, for equipment sold as recycling equipment, lists it beside acid content and moisture, so the rule treats it as a contaminant with its own limits.
reason: Explanation matched to the patched back.

value: The page gives nitrogen as its example of a method needing later purging. The rule itself draws the line by boiling point: above 85 °F at 29.9 inches of mercury, nitrogen may follow heat.
reason: Read alone, the card suggests R-113 is the only case where nitrogen is allowed, which clashes with the §82.156(a)(1)(ii) boiling-point test on the neighbouring cards.
